 The Average Social Security Recipient Could Get $900 More in 2027 (Here's the Catch)
 Chris Lewis, CEPF 2026년 11월 5일 목 오후 4:35 UTC 0 
Millions of Americans currently receiving Social Security are set to get a raise
in 2027. On October 14th, the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6%
cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), the largest increase since 2023, set to take
effect in January 2027. That would increase the average retired worker's monthly
benefit from $2,095 to approximately $2,170.
That's an extra $75 per month, or roughly $900 over the year, before deductions.
For retirees trying to stretch
 their retirement dollars, the increase offers some welcome relief from
higher living expenses.
Read on to learn more about the 2027 COLA and its impact on rising Medicare
premiums.
 Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 Who gets the raise and when it starts
The increase applies to nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries,
starting with January payments. About 7.3 million people on Supplemental
Security Income (SSI) would receive their benefits a little earlier, on Dec. 31,
2026. Some people collect both benefits.
Retired couples who both receive benefits would see a bigger dollar increase. The
SSA estimates the average monthly benefit for those couples would rise from
$3,238 to $3,355. That works out to about $117 more a month, or a little over
$1,400 a year.
Disabled workers and widowed retirees get smaller dollar increases because their
average benefits are lower. The average benefit for a disabled worker increases
from $1,642 to $1,701 per month. For an aged widow or widower collecting alone,
the average goes from $1,936 to $2,005. For SSI, the maximum federal payment for
an individual goes from $994 to $1,029 a month.

 How the SSA calculated the 3.6% increase
The Social Security Act sets a formula tied to the Consumer Price Index for
Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), an inflation measure that the
Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes monthly. It's that formula that determines
the annual increase percentage.
For 2027, the SSA compared the average CPI-W for July, August, and September 2026
with the same three months of 2025. That average rose 3.6%, so benefits go up by
the same percentage. The 2027 increase is up from 2.8% in 2026. It's also the
sixth year in a row with a COLA of 2.5% or more.
 How Medicare premiums reduce your COLA
If you're enrolled in Medicare, part of the raise would likely go toward a higher
premium. Most people on Medicare have their Part B premium deducted
automatically from their Social Security payment. When that premium goes up,
your deposit goes up by less than the COLA.
The Part B premium is set separately from the COLA. The standard premium is
$202.90 a month in 2026, up $17.90 from $185 in 2025. CMS announced those
figures on Nov. 14, 2025, and the 2027 premium hasn't been announced yet.

In June, the Medicare trustees projected the standard premium would rise to
$209.50 in 2027, an increase of $6.60. If the final number matches that
projection, the average retired worker's deposit would go up by about $68 a
month instead of $75. Higher-income enrollees pay more. About 8% of people with
Part B pay income-related surcharges, which could push the 2026 premium as high
as $689.90 per month.

 Why bigger benefits get bigger raises
The SSA raises each benefit by about 3.6% of its current amount, so a $1,500
monthly benefit goes up by about $54, while a $3,000 monthly benefit goes up by
about $108. Benefits are based on a worker's earnings record, so people who
earned more over their careers usually get larger raises in dollar terms.
That gap reappears when premiums rise. If the Part B premium goes up $6.60 as
projected, it would take about 12% of the $54 raise but only about 6% of the
$108 raise.
 Why some say the 2027 COLA still isn't enough
The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), a senior advocacy group, argues that COLAs
tied to the CPI-W index haven't kept up with the prices retirees actually pay.
For its 2026 Loss of Buying Power study, TSCL priced 70 goods and services the
way a senior living only on Social Security might shop. By its count, those
prices rose about 43.6% from 2016 to 2026, while the CPI-W rose 37.6%.
TSCL estimates that benefits have lost 13.7% of their buying power since 2016.
Making that up would take a 15.7% increase, or about $296 a month for the
average beneficiary. Basing the COLA on a different index would require Congress
to change the law.
 How to find your exact 2027 payment
The SSA would send each beneficiary a one-page notice with the exact new benefit
amount, payment dates, and any deductions. People with a my Social Security
account would see it online starting in late November, up to three weeks before
paper notices arrive. Medicare enrollees would also find their 2027 premium
amount in the account's Message Center.
Account holders are able to receive a text or email alert when the notice is
posted. If you haven't signed up for paperless notices, your COLA notice could come by mail in December.

 Bottom line
The 3.6% COLA adds about $75 a month to the average retired worker's benefit in
2027. If the Part B premium rises as projected by the Medicare trustees, someone
on Medicare with an average benefit would keep about $68 of the increase.
Keep in mind that Income taxes could take part of the raise, too. If your income
plus half your benefits tops $25,000 as a single filer or $32,000 filing
jointly, part of your benefits is taxable, and those limits aren't adjusted for
inflation. So each COLA moves some retirees closer to them. Planning around
those limits may help you keep more cash in your
 wallet.
